summary: The angels repeat the promise of Isaac to Abraham and Sarah, while Sodom is judged and Lot escapes. The chapter recounts Isaac’s birth and circumcision, then returns to Sarah’s pregnancy before describing Abraham’s seven-day celebration in booths as the beginning of Israel’s feast of tabernacles.
whyItMatters: The long-awaited child arrives, and the book anchors another annual festival in an ancestral event while also confronting the destructive judgment on Sodom.

context.author: Within the book, the angel of the presence dictates the account to Moses; the historical writer is unnamed.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through Moses in the book’s frame; the specific first historical audience is not identified.
context.date: The narrative places the revelation at Sinai; the historical Hebrew work is usually dated to the second century BCE, without an established exact year.
context.setting: Mamre, the region of Sodom, and Abraham's household near the Well of the Oath.
context.literaryForm: Ancestral narrative with judgment, birth announcement, and an origin story for a festival.

before.text: Sarah has been promised a son named Isaac, and Abraham’s household has received the covenant sign.

here.text: Isaac is born and the family’s joy becomes the book’s origin story for a seven-day booths festival.

after.text: Isaac’s weaning feast is followed by Hagar and Ishmael’s expulsion and a new test proposed by Mastêmâ.

outline.heading: Isaac’s birth announced to Sarah
outline.note: The angels repeat the promise and Sarah reacts.

outline.heading: Sodom judged and Lot spared
outline.note: The account joins rescue to a severe condemnation of Lot’s later conduct.

outline.heading: Sarah conceives and Isaac is born
outline.note: The promised son is born and circumcised; the angels speak of his line.

outline.heading: Abraham celebrates in booths
outline.note: Seven days of offerings and joy become an ancestral festival.

outline.heading: The feast assigned to Israel
outline.note: The angel names yearly practices and Abraham’s branches around the altar.

keyVerses.text: And she bare a son in the third month, and in the middle of the month, at the time of which the Lord had spoken to Abraham, on the festival of the first fruits of the harvest, Isaac was born.
keyVerses.why: Isaac’s birth is explicitly dated to the first-fruits festival and fulfills the earlier promise to Sarah.

keyVerses.text: And he built booths for himself and for his servants on this festival, and he was the first to celebrate the feast of tabernacles on the earth.
keyVerses.why: Abraham’s booths are identified as the first earthly celebration of the feast in the book’s telling.

questions.question: How does Sarah respond to the announcement?
questions.answer: She laughs on hearing the promise, becomes afraid when corrected, and denies having laughed. The angels nonetheless state the child’s name and the appointed time, keeping the promise central.

questions.question: What wrong does the chapter attribute to Sodom?
questions.answer: It gives a broad condemnation of wickedness, sexual misconduct, and defilement before describing the cities’ destruction. It does not detail each person’s actions here, so later assumptions should not be inserted as if this chapter had narrated them.

questions.question: Does Lot’s rescue mean the chapter approves all his later conduct?
questions.answer: No. The angel says Lot was saved because God remembered Abraham and immediately condemns the act involving Lot and his daughters. Rescue and moral approval are kept distinct in the text.

questions.question: How does Isaac’s birth connect to the previous covenant sign?
questions.answer: The child is born to Sarah at the promised time, and Abraham circumcises him on the eighth day. The narrative thus joins the named heir to the practice commanded in chapter 15.

questions.question: What is the “feast of tabernacles” here?
questions.answer: It is a seven-day celebration in temporary booths, accompanied in this account by offerings and thanksgiving. The angel later tells Israel to celebrate it annually in the seventh month.

questions.question: Why do the angels distinguish Isaac’s line from Abraham’s other sons?
questions.answer: They say other sons will become peoples, but that a line from Isaac will be set apart for God. This is the book’s account of Israel’s special role, not a denial that Abraham’s other descendants are human or capable of blessing.

questions.question: What practices does the festival account give Israel?
questions.answer: The angel names seven days of joy, dwelling in booths, wreaths, and leafy branches, with Abraham’s procession as a precedent. The instructions grow from his celebration rather than arriving as a detached list.

glossary.def: Temporary booths associated here with a seven-day harvest-season festival.
The beginning of the harvest, used in the narrative to date Isaac’s birth.
